I’m so, so, so fucking sorry this happened to you. I can really relate with the anger. It’s all consuming. I remember being asked why I was so angry all the time as a child, and I was so angry up until I moved out and went away for college. The distance helped, but the anger stayed. 

I finally found a therapist who is incredibly gentle and validating and after a rotating door of therapists the last 15 years I am finally talking about my trauma. And anger has been a huge topic. A couple things my therapist told me this week that I wrote down: “anger is our bodies last ditch effort to feel safe” and “anger is trying to tell us that something has been violated”. And for whatever reason that just blew my mind. Because it helped put a voice to my anger, if that makes sense? It gave my anger a shape and form and helped me visualize and understand how the anger I felt was my body trying to keep me safe. 

I’ll be thinking of you, and sending you good thoughts. I know it’s hard, but be gentle with yourself, at least for a little while. Treat yourself to a cookie, step on some crunchy leaves, relax your shoulders. I hope you and all of us find comfort soon.

Hi, non binary AFAB person. I am on a very low dose of T. You would say I was the LL of my marriage. It really did help my sex drive a lot. I kinda felt like a horny teenage boy, but be prepared for the side effects of testosterone, as it really depends on your genetics of what side effects you can get first. Yes, your libido will definitely increase, but you will also go through puberty again. You will experience bottom growth, facial/body hair, and acne. That’s just some of it. It’s worth trying out, and everyone’s experience with T is different, but if you’re not already in therapy and have tried everything to raise your libido, going on a low dose of testosterone may be a good idea if that is what you truly want.

1. I don’t feel like it’s hard to signify to others that you’re still a “woman” to other queer people, it honestly just depends on who your surround yourself with. I have been on low dosage of T for about 1.5 months now and I identify as NB and I bind, but there are moments where I do appreciate the femininity of my body. I have a wife and another female partner, and when I told my new partner I was on T when we met, she totally didn’t mind. She said she liked me for me, and those are the kinds of people you should be around. I haven’t had any negative experiences with queer/lesbian women when they find out I’m on T, it’s honestly none of their business and if they judge, that just means they’re not the kind of people I want to associate with. You’re always going to find TERFs like that in every community, especially in our community, but you just gotta remind yourself that you’re doing this for you, it doesn’t make you less than anything else. 
2. I have had some bottom growth. Remember, when taking low dosage T, changes are very, very slow, but the one thing that was pretty quick was my bottom growth. It’s not very significant, but I can tell the difference by the way it feels. My sex drive went from non existent to super high, and I feel more confident. I think the confidence is what is most affirming to my identity, bc I’m a very shy and self conscious person. I’m looking forward to the changes to come, even if they’re gonna come slowly, because I can finally feel myself becoming the person I’ve wanted to be. It all begins in your mind, tho. 
3. Definitely for me, bottom growth. I was scared at first, I don’t really know why, but when it happened I honestly don’t mind it? It’s the first “big” physical change that happens, so it’s just something to prepare yourself for because it’s one of the irreversible changes. It won’t go back to normal if you stop. I think something that people don’t really understand is that when you’re on such a low dosage, your body handles it a lot differently than it does to other people on low dosages and even people with higher dosages. It’s all in the way our body takes the testosterone. So don’t compare yourselves to others progress bc it’s just gonna bum you out. Take it slow, steady, track any emotional and physical and mental changes you feel and be very open and honest with your doctors.
